analysis.one_liner: Repeals the law requiring federal service contractors to pay workers prevailing wages and benefits.
analysis.headline: The bill to repeal federal service contract workers' wage floor drew 35 Republican cosponsors and cleared a House subcommittee in March 1995, but never received a full committee or floor vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This one-sentence bill would wipe the Service Contract Act of 1965 off the books [S2][S3]. That law requires companies winning federal service contracts — cleaning, food service, security, groundskeeping — to pay their workers wage rates and fringe benefits that the Labor Department sets for each job and region. The bill would have lifted that floor for all future contracts, while leaving existing contracts covered (section 2) [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Companies holding federal service contracts would gain. They could pay janitors, cafeteria workers, security guards, and groundskeepers whatever the market allows instead of government-set prevailing wages and benefits, cutting their labor costs and letting them bid lower or widen their margins on federal work. Taxpayers might see some savings if the lower costs actually showed up in contract bids, though that is not guaranteed.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the Service Contract Act of 1965 in its entirety, removing the legal requirement that federal service contractors pay government-set prevailing wages and fringe benefits to their employees [S2][S3].

For contractors, this means labor costs on federal cleaning, food service, security, and maintenance contracts are no longer tied to Labor Department wage determinations, so firms can cut pay and benefits, bid more aggressively for government work, or keep the difference as profit.
Section 2 grandfathers existing contracts, so repeal would apply only to contracts signed after enactment, giving contractors a transition rather than an immediate change [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The roughly hundreds of thousands of workers employed by federal service contractors — janitors, cafeteria and food service workers, security guards, laundry workers, groundskeepers — would bear the cost. The wage and benefit floor the government sets for these jobs would disappear, and in competitive bidding, contractors that underbid rivals would tend to cut labor costs to do it. These are predominantly low-wage workers with little individual bargaining power.

drawbacks.text: Repeal would remove the only wage and benefit floor specific to federal service contract work. Because federal contracts are repeatedly rebid, competitive pressure pushes companies toward the cheapest labor they can legally use, so workers in these jobs would face real risk of pay and benefit cuts [S3].

The strongest good-faith argument for repeal was that the Service Contract Act raises the cost of federal contracts, since contractors must build government-set wages and benefits into every bid; an honest supporter would have to concede that the people who absorb those costs are the workers themselves, not the companies.

Taxpayer savings from repeal are uncertain: in a competitive bid, savings from lower wages go to whichever firm wins, and there is no requirement that they be passed to the government in lower prices.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains flow to contractors in the form of lower labor costs and potentially to taxpayers if bids fall; the costs fall squarely on low-wage service workers whose pay and benefits would be set by the market alone. Because these workers have little bargaining power and their jobs are repeatedly rebid to the lowest bidder, the wage floor was doing real work for them. The bill offered nothing to offset that loss, making it a straightforward transfer of protection from workers to contractors.

outcome.mechanism: A House subcommittee approved it in March 1995, but the full committee never voted on it and it died when the two-year Congress ended without ever reaching the floor.

narrative.text: Representative Harris Fawell introduced the bill on January 4, 1995, with John Boehner and Cass Ballenger as original cosponsors; it was referred to the Committee on Economic and Educational Opportunities [S3][S5].
In February 1995 it went to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections, and the Labor Department was asked for its comments [S5].
On March 2, 1995, the subcommittee held a markup and forwarded the bill to the full committee with amendments [S5].
No further action is recorded: the full committee never reported the bill, and no House or Senate vote ever took place before the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Service workers on federal contracts are better off: the wage and benefit floor the bill would have removed stayed on the books. Federal service contractors did not get the repeal they sought.

sides.party_line_note: Every one of the 36 members behind the bill — the sponsor and 35 cosponsors — was a Republican, and no Democrat signed on; the bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call breakdown exists.

industries.industry: Federal service contractors (janitorial, food service, security, groundskeeping firms)
industries.note: Repeal would have freed these firms from paying government-set prevailing wages and benefits on federal contracts, cutting their labor costs. Their gain comes directly out of the pay of the low-wage workers they employ on government jobs.

industries.industry: Labor unions representing federal service workers
industries.note: The Service Contract Act's wage determinations underpin the pay standards these unions negotiate around; repeal would have removed that statutory floor and weakened their position in representing contract employees.
